questions.q: Why is idempotency mandatory, rather than a nice-to-have, in a real system design?
options: Because retries after a lost confirmation are unavoidable at scale, and a non-idempotent write silently corrupts data on a second run
Idempotency is only needed for streaming systems, never batch ones
Retries never actually happen in well-designed systems
Idempotency only matters for dimension tables, not fact tables
questions.explain: Databricks Lesson 29 named this directly: a non-idempotent pipeline silently corrupts data on a second run — retries make that scenario inevitable.

questions.q: What does an idempotency key actually do?
options: Lets the receiving system recognize a retry as the same logical operation, returning the original result instead of creating a duplicate
Encrypts the request so it can't be intercepted
Automatically retries a failed request a fixed number of times
Replaces the need for a primary key on the destination table
questions.explain: The caller generates it once per logical operation; a retry carrying the same key gets the original result back.

questions.q: Why is MERGE INTO the real mechanism behind idempotency, rather than just a definition?
options: Matching on a stable key, a reprocessed batch updates existing rows instead of inserting duplicates — plain append has no such protection
MERGE INTO is only available in streaming pipelines, not batch ones
MERGE INTO always deletes the entire table before rewriting it
MERGE INTO cannot be used with fact tables
questions.explain: Databricks Lesson 22 introduced MERGE INTO's syntax, and Lesson 29 showed why matching on a stable key is what actually prevents duplicate rows on a rerun.

questions.q: Why must a MERGE statement's ON clause match on a natural key rather than a surrogate key, for idempotency?
options: A surrogate key generated fresh on each load isn't stable across retries, so it can't reliably identify 'the same row' a second time
Natural keys are always integers, which MERGE requires
Surrogate keys cannot be used in SQL at all
There is no real difference between natural and surrogate keys for this purpose
questions.explain: The natural key (like the source's own order_id) exists before the row reaches you and stays stable across every retry; a surrogate key does not.

questions.q: How do dimension tables typically use surrogate keys, compared to how fact table dedup logic must work?
options: Dimensions commonly use surrogate keys for join performance, but merge/dedup logic must key off the natural identifier the source system provides
Dimensions and fact tables both require surrogate keys for dedup
Surrogate keys are never used anywhere in a star schema
Natural keys are only used in OLTP systems, never in dimensional models
questions.explain: Star schema dimensions (Lesson 8) use surrogate keys internally for join performance — a separate concern from keeping a fact table's MERGE idempotent.
